title: Skill Acquisition: From Goal-Directed to Habitual
excerpt: The exploration-exploitation section described how the basal ganglia manage uncertainty and generate behavioral variability when contingencies are unknown. But the most consequential transformation the BG orchestrate is not a single decision under uncertainty;
html:
The exploration-exploitation section described how the basal ganglia manage uncertainty and generate behavioral variability when contingencies are unknown. But the most consequential transformation the BG orchestrate is not a single decision under uncertainty; it is the long-arc process by which a novel, effortful, outcome-sensitive behavior is gradually compiled into a fast, stereotyped, and largely outcome-insensitive skill or habit. This transformation recruits, in sequence and in parallel, virtually every mechanism described in the preceding subsections: ventral striatal critic signals, dorsomedial flexible action-outcome learning, dorsolateral sequence crystallization, territory-specific plasticity regimes, distributional and multi-timescale error signals, opponent D1/D2 pathway dynamics, cholinergic gating, and the progressive remodeling of corticostriatal synaptic architecture. Tracing the full arc from goal-directed exploration to automatized execution therefore serves as the integrative case study for the BG optimization architecture. The process is best described not as a discrete three-stage pipeline but as a continuous, overlapping redistribution of influence across striatal territories and cortico-basal ganglia loops; for clarity, however, it is organized here into three broadly sequential phases that correspond to distinguishable behavioral and neural signatures.

Phase 1: Goal-directed acquisition (ventral and dorsomedial dominance). Early in learning, the organism confronts an environment whose action-outcome contingencies are unknown or poorly estimated. The computational demands at this stage are dominated by two problems: evaluating whether the current state of the world is worth engaging with, and discovering which actions produce which outcomes. These two problems map onto the ventral and dorsomedial striatal loops, respectively, and the neural and synaptic evidence reviewed in preceding sections converges on the conclusion that both are maximally engaged during early acquisition.

The ventral striatum, operating as the critic side of the actor-critic architecture, provides the initial value scaffolding. Ventral striatal neurons encode state value and reward expectation, and the dopaminergic prediction errors they help generate are largest and most information-rich during early learning, when outcomes are maximally surprising. Recent primate work by Fujimoto, Bhatt, Bhatt, and colleagues extends this picture by showing that ventral striatal neurons do not merely passively encode value but actively transform value representations into action-selection signals: single-unit activity initially reflects the value of an offered option and then gradually shifts, within a trial, to reflect the monkey’s upcoming choice, as though the ventral striatum itself bridges valuation and commitment 1. Optogenetic facilitation of dopamine input to the ventral striatum, as well as electrical stimulation of this region, causally altered the monkeys’ action selection, confirming that the ventral striatum is not merely a passive value register but an active participant in the conversion of motivational evaluation into behavioral output 1. This finding dovetails with the actor-critic analysis in the loss-function section: the ventral striatum is critic-like in its dominant concern with state value, but it is not purely a critic—it contributes directly to the process by which value information is translated into the policy biases that determine which action is actually selected. During early learning, when value estimates are volatile and action-outcome mappings are being established for the first time, this bridging function is presumably at its most consequential. This recent study illustrates fig. 2 Neural signatures of option valuation and action selection in the ventral striatum (Figure).

Meanwhile, the dorsomedial striatum supports the flexible, goal-directed component of early learning. DMS neurons encode action-outcome contingencies and are sensitive to outcome devaluation and contingency degradation—the hallmarks of goal-directed control 2, 3. At the network level, using in vivo recordings during rotarod skill learning, Yin, Mulcare, and colleagues showed that DMS neural activity is preferentially elevated during the early phase of training, with task-related firing rates in DMS peaking during the first sessions and declining thereafter 4. Ex vivo recordings from DMS slices of early-trained mice revealed changes in excitatory synaptic transmission consistent with rapid corticostriatal potentiation, confirming that the early DMS engagement has a synaptic substrate 4. At finer resolution, Badreddine, Bhatt, and colleagues used ex vivo two-photon calcium imaging to show that early training produces a distinctive DMS network signature: overall population activity decreases, but a small, sparsely distributed subset of highly active (HA) neurons emerges, and the size of this HA population correlates with individual learning performance 5. The sparsity and rapid turnover of DMS ensembles during early learning is consistent with the symmetric anti-Hebbian STDP regime described in the plasticity section, which favors flexible rewriting of corticostriatal weights over durable stabilization 6. Targeted silencing of these DMS HA cells with the cFos-TRAP strategy strongly impaired individual performance, confirming that the sparse early-phase DMS ensemble is not an epiphenomenon but a functional requirement for skill acquisition 5. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The dopaminergic teaching signal during this phase is large, bidirectional, and information-rich. In DMS-projecting dopamine terminals, prediction errors operate on intermediate temporal horizons and are sensitive to action-outcome contingencies 7, 8. The indirect pathway of the DMS is simultaneously active: as described in the exploration section, DMS iSPNs monitor the reliability of the current action policy and generate exploratory switches when outcomes are worse than expected 9. During reversal or contingency change, iSPN-dependent updating is specifically required 10. The cholinergic gating regime in DMS is reward-timed: dopamine transients that lag cholinergic dips at the offer cue predict trial-to-trial behavioral updating, consistent with a plasticity-promoting teaching mode 11. In summary, Phase 1 is characterized by large prediction errors, flexible corticostriatal rewriting in DMS, active ventral striatal value-to-action bridging, indirect-pathway-mediated exploration and policy revision, and behavior that is sensitive to outcome value and contingency structure. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Phase 2: Consolidation and the dorsomedial-to-dorsolateral transfer. With continued practice, a progressive shift occurs in which the dorsolateral striatum assumes an increasingly dominant role in behavioral control, while DMS engagement wanes. This shift is among the most replicated findings in basal ganglia neuroscience, having been documented with lesions, recordings, pharmacology, and imaging across species and task types 4, 12, 13. In the Yin et al. rotarod study, in vivo recordings showed that DLS task-related neural activity was low during early training but increased progressively with practice, reaching its highest levels during the late, consolidated phase of skill learning—the temporal inverse of the DMS pattern 4. Ex vivo recordings confirmed that this late-phase DLS engagement was accompanied by long-lasting potentiation of glutamatergic transmission, and—critically—this potentiation was preferentially expressed in striatopallidal (D2-expressing, indirect-pathway) neurons rather than striatonigral neurons 4. This pathway-specific finding is notable because it resonates with the opponent plasticity framework: in DLS, progressive D2-pathway potentiation may reflect the stabilization of action-suppression representations that protect the consolidated skill from interference by competing motor programs, consistent with the DLS’s known role in behaviors that are resistant to extinction and insensitive to outcome devaluation 14. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

At the network level, the DLS reorganization follows a qualitatively different trajectory than DMS. Whereas DMS produces a sparse, transient ensemble that is rapidly remodeled, DLS develops a progressive and long-lasting formation of spatially clustered highly active cell groups whose size and density increase monotonically with training duration 5. Importantly, these DLS clusters arise not merely from synaptic strengthening but from anatomical rearrangements—changes in the spatial organization of responsive neurons—suggesting that the consolidation of skill in DLS involves structural remodeling of the corticostriatal network, not merely functional reweighting of existing connections 5. This structural plasticity extends to the presynaptic side: recent longitudinal two-photon imaging of motor cortical axonal boutons in the DLS of awake mice showed that motor learning induces a transient burst of new bouton formation followed by selective stabilization of boutons responsive to rewarded movements and elimination of those responsive to unrewarded movements 15. The structural dynamics of DLS learning are therefore bidirectional and functionally selective: the circuit does not merely add connections; it prunes unrewarded pathways while consolidating rewarded ones, yielding a progressively more refined and movement-specific corticostriatal architecture. The 2025 longitudinal imaging results illustrate this training-linked structural plasticity (Figure). The 2025 longitudinal imaging results illustrate this training-linked structural plasticity (Figure).

The anatomical substrate for the DMS-to-DLS transfer has classically been attributed to the spiraling striato-nigro-striatal architecture described by Haber and colleagues, in which ventral striatal territories influence progressively more dorsal dopamine populations through ascending loops 16. As noted in the error-signal section, the strongest version of this spiral model has been tempered by evidence for both closed loops and more diffuse input organization, but the core principle—that ventral and medial striatal value signals can indirectly shape dopaminergic teaching in dorsolateral territories—remains the best available account of how value learning in one loop can progressively tutor policy learning in another. Complementing this indirect route, the dopamine signal itself changes character across the transfer. In DLS, dopamine dynamics are the fastest of any striatal territory, integrating reward history over the fewest trials and reflecting the steepest temporal discounting 7. Moreover, dopamine signals in DLS are positively shifted: reward responses remain non-negative even for outcomes worse than expected, and clear inhibitory dips to negative prediction errors are absent or strongly attenuated 8. This positive bias means that the effective teaching signal in DLS preferentially stamps in actions that were at least minimally successful, without erasing them when outcomes occasionally fall short—a property ideally suited to the consolidation of a well-practiced skill that should be robust to occasional failure. The asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP regime in DLS further supports this stability: as described in the plasticity section, DLS plasticity rules favor memory maintenance over memory flexibility, providing a synaptic correlate of the behavioral transition from outcome-sensitive to outcome-insensitive control 6. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The cholinergic regime in DLS likewise shifts. Whereas DMS cholinergic dynamics are reward-timed and plasticity-promoting, DLS cholinergic interneuron activity is more movement-timed: CIN bursts coincide with movement events rather than reward events, and coincident dopamine predicts the vigor of upcoming movements without evidence of lasting plasticity 11, 17. This transition from a learning mode to a performance/vigor mode in the local neuromodulatory environment is consistent with the broader shift from policy updating to policy execution that characterizes the DMS-to-DLS transfer.

A crucial point, emphasized in the user’s notes and supported by recent evidence, is that the DMS-to-DLS transfer is not a simple serial handoff. Both territories are simultaneously active throughout learning, but they develop different task-related patterns with different dynamics. The Vandaele, Bhatt, and colleagues study found that, contrary to the canonical expectation, distinct DMS and DLS activity patterns were present during early training but converged with extended training, and performance after extended training was not associated with DMS disengagement 18. Even more strikingly, Turner and colleagues showed that DMS and DLS can compete for behavioral control: in a five-step heterogeneous action sequencing task optimized for habitual responding, DMS lesions accelerated sequence acquisition—rats became faster, more accurate, and more stereotyped sooner–whereas DLS lesions impeded it 19. This result is difficult to reconcile with a purely cooperative model and instead supports a competitive-opposition account in which DMS-mediated goal-directed control actively gates or restrains the transition to DLS-mediated automaticity. The implication is that the DMS does not simply hand off control to DLS when its job is done; rather, DMS continuously competes with DLS for behavioral expression, and the shift toward habitual control reflects a change in the balance of this competition–a balance that is itself regulated by the dopaminergic, cholinergic, and cortical inputs that set the relative excitability and plasticity of the two territories. The lateral orbitofrontal cortex, but not medial prefrontal cortex, was found to be critical for this balance, suggesting that cortical evaluation of action outcomes feeds into the competitive dynamics between striatal subregions 19.

Phase 3: Crystallization, chunking, and cortical disengagement. The final phase of the goal-directed-to-habitual arc is the crystallization of individual actions into concatenated sequences that are processed as single behavioral units ("chunks") and the progressive transfer of motor-program specification from cortical to subcortical circuits. This phase represents the endpoint of BG policy optimization for a given skill: the policy is no longer being searched or revised; it is being compiled into a format that minimizes the computational and metabolic cost of execution. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The neural signature of chunking in the DLS is the task-bracketing pattern: with extensive training, DLS neurons develop concentrated activity at the initiation and termination of well-learned action sequences, with suppressed or below-baseline activity during the interior of the sequence 12, 20. This pattern has been replicated across maze navigation, lever-pressing, and oculomotor tasks in rodents and primates 12, and it is remarkably durable: reward devaluation after prolonged overtraining hardly changes it, and even extinction (complete reward removal) only temporarily suppresses it–the pattern reappears almost immediately when rewards are reinstated, indicating that the underlying synaptic architecture is latent but not erased 12. This extinction-resistance is precisely what the DLS plasticity regime predicts: asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP, positively biased dopamine signals, and progressive structural consolidation of corticostriatal ensembles all favor durable, extinction-resistant memory traces 6, 8. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The task-bracketing pattern is computationally significant because it implies that the DLS treats the entire action sequence as a single macro-action, with explicit representations only at the boundaries. In reinforcement-learning terms, this is hierarchical chunking: instead of selecting each element of a sequence independently (which would require a separate selection-evaluation cycle for every action), the BG select the chunk as a unit, and the internal elements are executed ballistically under local motor-circuit control. This dramatically reduces the computational and metabolic cost of action selection by collapsing a multi-step decision problem into a single policy choice. The start signal disinhibits a cortical or subcortical motor program that itself specifies the temporal sequence of sub-elements; the stop signal terminates it and returns control to the higher-level selection process. The anti-Hebbian STDP rule in DLS is computationally suited for encoding the temporal order within these chunks: Vignoud and colleagues showed that anti-Hebbian plasticity, when combined with the characteristic spike latency and collateral inhibition of SPNs, enables striatal circuits to learn spike sequences, providing a synaptic-level mechanism for how temporal order is written into DLS representations 21. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The DLS does not, however, only mark sequence boundaries. Dhawale, Wolff, Ko, and Ölveczky showed that the sensorimotor arm of the basal ganglia circuit specifies and controls the fine-grained kinematic details of learned motor skills, not merely their initiation and termination 22. DLS neurons encoded the detailed movement trajectories of well-trained rats on a trial-by-trial basis, and lesioning DLS abolished the idiosyncratic kinematic signatures of the learned skill—the animals could still move, but the specific, stereotyped movement patterns they had acquired through training were lost 22. Importantly, these DLS representations and the control functions they subserve did not depend on inputs from motor cortex: even after motor cortex lesions, striatal neural activity retained its sequential, kinematic-encoding structure 22. This result extends the BG’s role beyond action selection and chunking to encompass the continuous, moment-by-moment shaping of movement kinematics during automatized execution.

This last finding connects to one of the most striking demonstrations of cortical disengagement during skill consolidation. Kawai, Ölveczky, and colleagues showed that motor cortex is required for learning a skilled motor sequence but not for executing it: motor cortex lesions performed after asymptotic training had no discernible effect on the acquired skill, which was expressed in its distinct pre-lesion form on the very first day of post-lesion testing 23. Hwang and colleagues extended this by showing that motor cortex gradually disengages from movement control over the course of long-term learning, with optogenetic inactivation of motor cortex producing progressively smaller behavioral deficits as training proceeds 24. The implication is that motor cortex serves as a "tutor" during skill acquisition–providing the rich, flexible corticostriatal drive that enables DMS-and then DLS-dependent learning–but that the ultimate repository of the learned motor program is subcortical, residing in the corticostriatal and thalamostriatal synaptic weights of DLS and in the downstream brainstem and spinal circuits that DLS modulates through its output via GPi/SNr 23, 22, 25. A recent perspective by Grillner formalizes this endpoint, proposing that the DLS-SNr-parafascicular thalamus-DLS loop, subdivided into many parallel channels with precise cortical input, constitutes the minimal circuit for storing and executing crystallized motor programs once cortical tutoring is complete 26.

The composite picture of the goal-directed-to-habitual arc can now be stated in the vocabulary of the preceding BG subsections. Early in learning, the ventral striatum provides the critic-like value scaffolding that converts motivational state into action-selection biases, while the DMS supports flexible, outcome-sensitive action-outcome learning through rapid corticostriatal rewriting under large, bidirectional dopaminergic prediction errors and cholinergic plasticity gating. With continued practice, the balance of influence shifts toward DLS–not through a discrete handoff but through a competitive rebalancing in which DMS goal-directed control progressively yields to DLS habitual control. The DLS develops spatially clustered, structurally consolidated corticostriatal ensembles under an asymmetric anti-Hebbian plasticity regime, positively biased dopamine signals, and movement-timed cholinergic dynamics. At the endpoint, individual actions have been concatenated into chunks marked by task-bracketing boundary signals, the fine-grained kinematics of the skill are specified by DLS representations operating through subcortical motor circuits, and the motor cortex that originally tutored the learning has largely disengaged from execution. The entire transformation can be read as a progression through the BG’s multi-timescale, territory-specific loss landscape: from a regime dominated by long-horizon, high-uncertainty, outcome-sensitive evaluation (ventral and dorsomedial loops) to a regime dominated by short-horizon, low-uncertainty, execution-optimized control (dorsolateral loops). This is the BG’s version of a curriculum—but where cortical learning curricula are typically organized over representational depth (and over developmental timescales), the BG curriculum is organized over policy type: from flexible, model-informed, goal-directed policies to rigid, stimulus-bound, automatized policies whose computational and metabolic cost of execution is minimized.
